CHAPTER 1.1 · LEARNING AREA 1 · AUGUST · SEPTEMBER

Vectors and the scalar product

A drone flies right across the classroom, a crane lifts a load against the wind, a sledge is pulled at an angle: anyone who wants to describe movements and forces in space needs vectors. You learn to calculate with them, to find lengths and to use the scalar product to measure angles and recognise right angles.

8 LESSONS3 UNITSREAL 3D1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • show points and vectors in a three-dimensional coordinate system, find position vectors and connecting vectors
  • calculate the magnitude of a vector, distances and midpoints
  • add, subtract and multiply vectors by a number, also geometrically
  • use the scalar product to calculate angles and check for orthogonality

Pythagoras: $\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$

Bottom right: the fourth quadrant.

What is $\cos 60^\circ$?

$\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$

Solve $2x - 4 = 0$.

$x = 2$

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Points and vectors in space

If you put the origin in the drone’s starting corner, the finish is at $C(8, 6, 3)$. The flight is the arrow from the origin to $C$, the vector $\vec{OC} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 6 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$. Its length: $\sqrt{8^2 + 6^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{109} \approx 10.44$ m.

In a three-dimensional coordinate system the $x$-axis points forwards, the $y$-axis to the right and the $z$-axis upwards. A point has three coordinates, $P(p_1, p_2, p_3)$. A vector describes a translation: all arrows that have the same length and point in the same direction represent the same vector. The arrow from the origin to a point is called its position vector, the arrow from $A$ to $B$ the connecting vector.

KEY POINT · VECTORS IN SPACE

Connecting vector: “tip minus tail”, $\vec{AB} = \vec{OB} - \vec{OA} = \begin{pmatrix} b_1 - a_1 \\ b_2 - a_2 \\ b_3 - a_3 \end{pmatrix}$

Magnitude (length): $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}$. The distance between two points is $|\vec{AB}|$.

Unit vector (length 1, same direction): $\vec{a}_0 = \dfrac{1}{|\vec{a}|} \cdot \vec{a}$

Midpoint of the line segment $AB$: $\vec{OM} = \tfrac12\,(\vec{OA} + \vec{OB})$

Oblique drawing: on paper the $x$-axis is drawn at a slant towards the bottom left and shortened, usually by the factor $\tfrac12\sqrt2$, about 0.7.

Notation: vectors are written as columns, points as coordinates in brackets. The point $P(2, 1, 3)$ has the position vector $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

INTERACTIVE · POINTS AND VECTORS IN 3D

Enter the coordinates of $A$ and $B$ and turn the coordinate system with the mouse or your finger. The dashed lines show how to reach the point from the $x$-$y$-plane.

EXAMPLE 1 · DISTANCE AND MIDPOINT

Given $A(1, 2, -1)$ and $B(4, -2, 11)$. Calculate the distance between the points and the midpoint of the line segment $AB$.

$\vec{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -4 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$, $|\vec{AB}| = \sqrt{9 + 16 + 144} = \sqrt{169}$: distance 13.

$\vec{OM} = \tfrac12 \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \\ 10 \end{pmatrix}$: $M(2.5, 0, 5)$

EXAMPLE 2 · UNIT VECTOR

Find the unit vector of $\vec{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

$|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$, so $\vec{a}_0 = \tfrac13 \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

Check: $\sqrt{\tfrac49 + \tfrac19 + \tfrac49} = 1$.

EXERCISES

Find $\vec{AB}$ and $|\vec{AB}|$ for $A(2, 0, 1)$ and $B(5, 4, 1)$.

$\vec{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $|\vec{AB}| = 5$

Calculate the magnitude: a) $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$   b) $\begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$   c) $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -5 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$

a) $3$   b) $\sqrt{49} = 7$   c) $\sqrt{169} = 13$

Calculate the length of the line segment $PQ$ and its midpoint for $P(-3, 5, 2)$ and $Q(1, -1, 6)$.

$\vec{PQ} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -6 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$, $|\vec{PQ}| = \sqrt{68} \approx 8.25$; $M(-1, 2, 4)$

For which numbers $t$ does the vector $\begin{pmatrix} t \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ have length 6?

Square the equation $\sqrt{t^2 + 4 + 16} = 6$.

$t^2 + 20 = 36 \Rightarrow t^2 = 16$: $t = 4$ or $t = -4$

A cuboid has one vertex at the origin and the edges 4, 3 and 2 along the axes. Calculate the length of the space diagonal and of the diagonal of the base. Use this to solve the exploration “The drone in the classroom” once more without vectors.

Opposite vertex $G(4, 3, 2)$: space diagonal $\sqrt{16 + 9 + 4} = \sqrt{29} \approx 5.39$, base $\sqrt{16 + 9} = 5$. Drone: floor diagonal $\sqrt{64 + 36} = 10$, then $\sqrt{10^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{109} \approx 10.44$ m. Pythagoras twice gives the same formula as the magnitude.

TEST YOURSELF!

How long is the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$?

$\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$

How far apart are $A(1, 1, 1)$ and $B(3, 5, 5)$?

$\vec{AB} = (2, 4, 4)$, length $\sqrt{36} = 6$

Which vector is a unit vector?

$0.36 + 0.64 = 1$

UNIT 22 LESSONS

2Calculating with vectors

A crane lifts a load with the force $\vec{F}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ kN, the wind pushes with $\vec{F}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ kN. The load is acted on by the sum $\vec{F}_1 + \vec{F}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ kN with the magnitude $\sqrt{30} \approx 5.48$ kN, less than $5 + \sqrt5 \approx 7.24$ kN.

Vectors are added by putting the arrows tip to tail. In coordinates this means: you add row by row. A multiple $r \cdot \vec{a}$ stretches or shrinks the arrow, a negative $r$ also reverses its direction.

KEY POINT · RULES OF CALCULATION

$\vec{a} + \vec{b} = \begin{pmatrix} a_1 + b_1 \\ a_2 + b_2 \\ a_3 + b_3 \end{pmatrix}$,   $r \cdot \vec{a} = \begin{pmatrix} r a_1 \\ r a_2 \\ r a_3 \end{pmatrix}$,   $\vec{a} - \vec{b} = \vec{a} + (-\vec{b})$

The commutative, associative and distributive laws hold as they do for numbers.

Two vectors are called collinear (parallel) if one is a multiple of the other: $\vec{b} = r \cdot \vec{a}$.

Parallelogram rule: $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$ is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, $\vec{a} - \vec{b}$ the other diagonal.

Zero vector: $\vec{a} + (-\vec{a}) = \vec{0}$. It has length 0 and no direction.

INTERACTIVE · SUM, DIFFERENCE, MULTIPLE

At the top you can switch between points, sum and difference, and multiples. Change the coordinates and watch the parallelogram move along.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE FOURTH VERTEX

$A(1, 0, 2)$, $B(4, 1, 2)$ and $C(5, 5, 3)$ are vertices of the parallelogram $ABCD$. Find $D$.

In the parallelogram $\vec{AD} = \vec{BC} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

$\vec{OD} = \vec{OA} + \vec{BC}$: $D(2, 4, 3)$

EXAMPLE 4 · COLLINEAR?

Are $\vec{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -4 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\vec{b} = \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 6 \\ -9 \end{pmatrix}$ collinear?

The first row gives $r = -1.5$. Check: $-1.5 \cdot (-4) = 6$ and $-1.5 \cdot 6 = -9$.

Yes, $\vec{b} = -1.5 \cdot \vec{a}$: parallel, but pointing in the opposite direction.

EXERCISES

Calculate: a) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$   b) $3 \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$

a) $\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$   b) $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -7 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$

Check for collinearity: a) $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$   b) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$

a) yes, factor 3   b) no: the first row requires $r = -2$, the third $r = -3$.

The centroid of a triangle is $\vec{OS} = \tfrac13\,(\vec{OA} + \vec{OB} + \vec{OC})$. Calculate it for $A(1, 2, 0)$, $B(5, 0, 3)$, $C(3, 7, 6)$.

$\tfrac13 \begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ 9 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$: $S(3, 3, 3)$

Find $r$ and $s$ such that $r \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} + s \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$.

The first two rows give $r$ and $s$ straight away. The third is the check.

$r = 3$, $s = -2$, check: $2 \cdot 3 + (-2) = 4$ ✔

A drone takes off at the origin and covers the vector $\vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \\ 1.2 \end{pmatrix}$ (in m) every 10 seconds. Where is it after 25 seconds? How fast is it flying?

After 25 s: $2.5 \cdot \vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 7.5 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$, so at the point $(10, 7.5, 3)$. Speed: $|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{26.44} \approx 5.14$ m in 10 s, about 0.51 m/s.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is the third coordinate of $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + 2 \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$?

$3 + 2 \cdot (-1) = 1$

$ABCD$ is a parallelogram with $A(0, 0, 0)$, $B(2, 0, 0)$, $C(3, 2, 1)$. What is the $y$-coordinate of $D$?

$\vec{OD} = \vec{OA} + \vec{BC} = (1, 2, 1)$

Which vector is collinear with $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$?

Factor $-3$

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3Scalar product, angles and orthogonality

A trolley rolls 20 m straight ahead, $\vec{s} = \begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ m. The rope pulls at a slant upwards with $\vec{F} = \begin{pmatrix} 30 \\ 0 \\ 15 \end{pmatrix}$ N. Only the part of the force in the direction of travel does work: $W = 30 \cdot 20 + 0 \cdot 0 + 15 \cdot 0 = 600$ J. Exactly this calculation is called the scalar product.

The scalar product of two vectors is a number. You work it out in coordinates. At the same time a geometric formula with the angle between the vectors holds. Rearranging it lets you calculate angles in space. And because $\cos 90^\circ = 0$, you recognise right angles by the scalar product being zero.

KEY POINT · SCALAR PRODUCT

$\vec{a} \circ \vec{b} = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3 = |\vec{a}| \cdot |\vec{b}| \cdot \cos \varphi$

Angle: $\cos \varphi = \dfrac{\vec{a} \circ \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}| \cdot |\vec{b}|}$ with $0^\circ \le \varphi \le 180^\circ$

Orthogonal: $\vec{a} \perp \vec{b} \iff \vec{a} \circ \vec{b} = 0$ (for vectors that are not the zero vector)

$\vec{a} \circ \vec{b} > 0$: acute angle · $\vec{a} \circ \vec{b} < 0$: obtuse angle · $\vec{a} \circ \vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2$

Notation: many books write $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$. Like the widgets, we write $\vec{a} \circ \vec{b}$, so that it is not confused with the multiple $r \cdot \vec{a}$.

On the graphing calculator: work out the angle with $\cos^{-1}$. Check first that the calculator is set to degrees (DEG).

INTERACTIVE · SCALAR PRODUCT AND ANGLE

Try the examples and vectors of your own. The dashed line is the perpendicular from the tip of $\vec{b}$ onto $\vec{a}$: it shows the part of $\vec{b}$ in the direction of $\vec{a}$.

EXAMPLE 5 · ANGLE BETWEEN VECTORS

Calculate the angle between $\vec{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\vec{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

$\vec{a} \circ \vec{b} = 2 - 2 + 4 = 4$, $|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| = 3$.

$\cos \varphi = \tfrac49$: $\varphi \approx 63.6^\circ$

EXAMPLE 6 · RIGHT-ANGLED TRIANGLE

Show that the triangle $A(1, 0, 0)$, $B(3, 2, 1)$, $C(0, 2, -2)$ has a right angle at $A$, and calculate the angle at $B$.

$\vec{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{AC} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{AB} \circ \vec{AC} = -2 + 4 - 2 = 0$ ✔

At $B$: $\vec{BA} \circ \vec{BC} = 9$, $|\vec{BA}| = 3$, $|\vec{BC}| = \sqrt{18}$, $\cos \beta = \tfrac{9}{3\sqrt{18}} \approx 0.707$: $\beta = 45^\circ$

EXERCISES

Calculate the scalar product: a) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \circ \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$   b) $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} \circ \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. What does the result of b) mean?

a) $8 - 3 + 5 = 10$   b) $3 - 6 + 3 = 0$: the vectors are perpendicular to each other.

For which $t$ are $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ t \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ orthogonal?

$6 - t + 4 = 0$: $t = 10$

Calculate the angle between $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

$\cos \varphi = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2 \cdot \sqrt2} = \tfrac12$: $\varphi = 60^\circ$

Give two different vectors that are orthogonal to $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and are not collinear with each other.

Set one coordinate to zero, swap the other two and change one sign.

For example $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$: $2 - 2 = 0$ and $3 - 3 = 0$.

In a cube: what angle does the space diagonal make with an edge? What angle do two space diagonals make with each other?

Put a cube with edge 1 at the origin: space diagonals $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, edge $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$.

With the edge: $\cos \varphi = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, $\varphi \approx 54.7^\circ$. Two space diagonals: $\cos \varphi = \tfrac13$, $\varphi \approx 70.5^\circ$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Calculate $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \circ \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

$3 + 0 - 3 = 0$: orthogonal

For which $t$ is $\begin{pmatrix} t \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} \perp \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}$?

$2t + 4 - 6 = 0$: $t = 1$

What angle do $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ make?

$\cos \varphi = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$: $45^\circ$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

How far is the point $P(2, -3, 6)$ from the origin?

$\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$

Connecting with Year 11: two lines in the plane with the gradients $m_1$ and $m_2$ are perpendicular if $m_1 \cdot m_2 = -1$. Explain this with the scalar product of the direction vectors $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ m_1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ m_2 \end{pmatrix}$.

Orthogonal means $1 \cdot 1 + m_1 m_2 = 0$, so $m_1 m_2 = -1$. Example: $m_1 = 2$ and $m_2 = -0.5$.

Show that $A(2, 0, 1)$, $B(4, 3, 1)$, $C(1, 5, 1)$, $D(-1, 2, 1)$ form a square.

Parallelogram ($\vec{AB} = \vec{DC}$), right angle ($\vec{AB} \circ \vec{AD} = 0$), sides of equal length.

$\vec{AB} = \vec{DC} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{AD} = \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{AB} \circ \vec{AD} = -6 + 6 = 0$, $|\vec{AB}| = |\vec{AD}| = \sqrt{13}$: a square.

A sledge is pulled 50 m. The rope pulls with 120 N at an angle of 30° to the track. Calculate the work done as a scalar product.

$\vec{s} = \begin{pmatrix} 50 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{F} = \begin{pmatrix} 120 \cos 30^\circ \\ 0 \\ 120 \sin 30^\circ \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 103.9 \\ 0 \\ 60 \end{pmatrix}$, $W = \vec{F} \circ \vec{s} \approx 5196$ J, about 5.2 kJ.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

The teacher who invented the vector

Hermann Grassmann (1809–1877) was a grammar school teacher in Stettin. In 1844 he published a book with the title “Die lineale Ausdehnungslehre, ein neuer Zweig der Mathematik” (the theory of linear extension, a new branch of mathematics). In it he calculated with directed line segments just as you do in this chapter: he added them, multiplied them by numbers and multiplied them with each other, not only in three but in any number of dimensions.

Hardly anyone understood the book. Grassmann never became a professor and turned to linguistics. Only decades later did mathematicians realise that he had laid the foundations of linear algebra, on which computer graphics, robotics and artificial intelligence are built today.

Source: H. Graßmann, “Die lineale Ausdehnungslehre, ein neuer Zweig der Mathematik”, Leipzig 1844. Biography and an extract from the preface: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

CONNECTING VECTOR

Tip minus tail: $\vec{AB} = \vec{OB} - \vec{OA}$

$A(1, 2, -1)$, $B(4, -2, 11)$: $\vec{AB} = (3, -4, 12)$

MAGNITUDE

$|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}$, distance between two points $= |\vec{AB}|$

$|(3, -4, 12)| = 13$

CALCULATING

Add and multiply row by row · collinear: $\vec{b} = r \cdot \vec{a}$

Midpoint $\vec{OM} = \tfrac12(\vec{OA} + \vec{OB})$

SCALAR PRODUCT

$\vec{a} \circ \vec{b} = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3 = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}| \cos \varphi$

$(1, 2, 2) \circ (2, -1, 2) = 4$, $\varphi \approx 63.6^\circ$

ORTHOGONAL

A scalar product of zero means a right angle.

$(1, -2, 3) \circ (3, 3, 1) = 0$
